Student training / understand it before selling it

The roofer doesn’t want
more follow-up.
They want more paid jobs.

This guide explains the buyer’s business, where money can be lost, and what our proposed system actually changes. The examples are illustrative. Confirm the problem with each owner rather than telling them what must be wrong.

1. Understand how the roofer gets paid

A homeowner enquires about replacing a roof. Someone qualifies the enquiry, visits the property, measures the job and prepares an estimate. The homeowner compares options and decides. The roofer agrees the work, collects the required payment, schedules the crew and completes the job.

The estimate is a step toward revenue. It is not revenue itself. An owner may have a large quote pipeline but very little cash arriving. Your offer helps move eligible open estimates toward a real decision and, where the job is won, payment.

2. Where the problem actually happens

Imagine a homeowner who likes the roofer but is unsure about timing. The rep sends the estimate, makes one follow-up call and moves on to new appointments. The homeowner doesn’t answer. Two weeks pass. The CRM still says “estimate sent.”

The owner cannot tell whether that person bought elsewhere, postponed the project, needs their partner involved or simply wants one question answered. The problem is the absence of a reliable next step—not necessarily a bad salesperson or a bad quote.

If the homeowner has already bought elsewhere, an automation will not recover the job. If they are still considering it, a relevant follow-up can create another opportunity to sell. That distinction is why the system needs replies, context and human handoffs rather than a blind message blast.

3. The pains to listen for

What the owner might sayThe underlying painWhat to ask
“We need more leads.”They may be paying to replace opportunities they never fully worked.“How many estimates from last month are still open, and what happens to them?”
“My reps only chase the hot ones.”Follow-up depends on individual habits. Older quotes have no consistent owner.“Who is responsible after the first follow-up doesn’t get a response?”
“I don’t know why we lost those jobs.”No useful objection data. Price, timing and trust issues get lumped together.“Can you show me the last three estimates marked lost and why?”
“We’ve got quotes everywhere but the schedule is patchy.”Pipeline value feels reassuring while sold work and cash are uncertain.“Which open estimates could you actually fulfil if they came back this week?”
“The office is flat out.”Repeat chasing competes with scheduling, customer support and current jobs.“What gets delayed when the office has to chase estimates?”
“We already have a CRM.”The tool may exist without a complete operating process—or it may already work well.“What happens when someone replies to an automated message?”
“I don’t want a bot making us look bad.”Reputation, wrong answers and unwanted follow-up are real concerns.“Which questions should always go straight to your team?”

4. What you are actually installing

  1. A usable list: eligible unsold estimates, each with its original quote, owner, last contact and current status. Remove sold jobs, firm losses, duplicates and opt-outs.
  2. A follow-up process: agreed messages at sensible intervals through approved channels, with a clear stopping point when the homeowner replies or the status changes.
  3. A reply handler: AI identifies the question or intent and uses approved information for routine answers. Uncertainty, pricing, financing, technical advice and complaints go to a person.
  4. A sales handoff: the rep receives the original estimate, the homeowner’s concern and a clear next action. The homeowner should not have to start the conversation again.
  5. An outcome record: track replies, held reviews, signed work and payments separately. This shows whether activity is becoming money.

The AI is useful because homeowner replies vary. The workflow handles predictable rules such as stopping on a sold job or assigning a task. You do not need to describe everything as AI. Explain the useful result of each part.

5. Before and after, in plain English

Before: “We sent an estimate. They didn’t answer. We’ll try again if someone remembers.”

After: “The homeowner is still interested but wants to discuss the start date. Their rep has the quote, the question and a scheduled next action. The system stops the generic follow-up.”

The commercial result you’re working toward: the rep wins suitable work, the customer pays, and the business gets more from the enquiries it already generated. More messages alone is not success.

6. What remains the roofer’s job

The roofer determines technical suitability, approves the price, answers specialist questions, confirms financing and availability, signs the agreement, fulfils the job and records payment. The system cannot make a poor quote competitive, create installation capacity or force a homeowner to buy.

You own the scoped implementation, monitoring, reply-routing quality and agreed follow-up work. Technical support helps confirm integrations and build them. It does not remove your responsibility to understand what you sold.

7. Why pay you if the software exists?

They pay for a working process: clean data, appropriate messaging, correct routing, staff adoption, exceptions and measurement. They can use an existing platform or another provider. If they already have this operating well, they are not your ideal customer.

Do not claim “your CRM can’t do this.” JobNimbus supports automated messages; Hatch offers broader AI follow-up. Ask what actually happens inside the business and demonstrate the part that is missing. A reminder setting alone does not justify a full recovery programme.

8. Explain the offer in 30 seconds

“You’ve already paid for the enquiries and sent the estimates. We set up and run the follow-up that finds out who is still interested, handles the routine replies and brings those homeowners back to your reps. Your team closes the jobs. We track the result through to collected payments, and agree a recovery target before starting.”

9. How to explain the work-free commitment

“If we miss the agreed recovery target, we keep doing the agreed follow-up work without charging a management fee until we hit it.”

Before promising this, define the eligible cohort, target, deadline, access and sales responsibilities. State that software costs still apply. Collected cash must be checked against payment records and net of refunds. A signed contract, a reply or a booking does not equal money received.

The target is not an arbitrary number copied from an ad. Assess the real pipeline and likely contribution. Continued free work has a delivery cost: include that downside in your private commercial assessment.

10. What to show on a sales call

  1. A clearly labelled sample unsold estimate and why it qualifies.
  2. The follow-up the homeowner would receive.
  3. Three replies: interested, not interested, and a question requiring a person.
  4. The correct stop or human handoff for each reply.
  5. How sold work and collected payment are recorded separately.

Use a connected sandbox to demonstrate the actual implementation before claiming it works. The current page storyboard explains the proposed process; it is not that technical proof.

Teach-back before the strategy call

Can you explain who buys, what happens today, where the pain comes from, what changes, what stays human and why the owner would pay? Can you name a situation where this is the wrong service? If those answers are unclear, return to the workflow and buyer conversation before writing more ads.
